articles.title: Wild chimpanzees teach youngsters by handing them tools
articles.summary: Adult chimpanzees have been observed passing tools to their younger relatives, helping them learn the skills needed for fishing for ants or algae
articles.content:
Adult chimpanzees have been observed passing tools to their younger relatives, helping them learn the skills needed for fishing for ants or algae

An infant chimpanzee (left) observing how two adults (centre) dip for army ants while another infant (right) takes a tool from one of the adults Jane Goodall Institute Spain

Wild adult chimpanzees have been seen passing tools to youngsters to help them learn and then coaching them, supporting the idea that teaching helps immature chimps acquire technological skills.

“To actually catch it on film is important and was very surprising for us,” says R. Adriana Hernandez-Aguilar at the University of Barcelona, Spain.

Chimpanzees are known to make and use a variety of tools, from leaf or moss sponges that soak up water to sticks used to fish for army ants or algae, and even crafting simple spears for hunting. But how chimpanzees learn such skills is debated.

Advertisement

It is clear that the knowledge does get passed on. For example, one study showed an increase in the number of chimps in Uganda using moss as a sponge to soak up water from a pond. Work with captive chimps has also shown that the animals can pass on knowledge to others. The big question is whether individuals copy behaviour after observation, actively teach each other or independently come up with the same solutions to a task.

To see if they could answer that, Hernandez-Aguilar and her colleagues analysed 15 hours of footage from camera traps at the Jane Goodall Institute’s biological station in Dindefelo, Senegal, taken between 2017 and 2025. The cameras were placed near 14 sites in the area where wild western chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes verus) had previously been recorded using tools, including fishing for algae, army ants and termites.

In total, the camera traps recorded 33 instances of tool transfer from one chimp to another: 19 when they were dipping for ants to eat, 10 during fishing for algae and four when fishing for termites. Generally, a chimp handed the key object to a close relative, and in 30 per cent of cases, this was from a mother to her offspring.

In one video, a mother, Soukki, inserted a dipping stick into an ant nest, then grabbed her baby daughter, Saïsaï, and led her to the tool. Saïsaï pulled the stick out and ate the ants clinging to it.

“We found support for the idea that tool transfers are a form of teaching that experienced chimpanzees may use to facilitate the learning of young individuals,” says team member Andreu Sánchez-Megías, also at the University of Barcelona.

An infant chimpanzee (centre) observing how a juvenile (right) pounds a baobab fruit against a rocky outcrop Jane Goodall Institute Spain

The team also gathered 30 minutes of footage from cameras at 11 sites where chimpanzees pound hard-shelled baobab fruit against stones to crack them open. This is considered proto-tool use rather than tool use, because the stones are being used as an anvil rather than being directly held and manipulated.

In an example of this, a mother called Féré collected three baobab fruits and placed them near her infant son Fotti. A juvenile male – probably an older sibling – picked up a fruit and pounded it against some rocks while Fotti watched, then guided Fotti’s hand to a fruit. Fotti had a go himself, eventually managing to open up a fruit.

The videos support the idea that other social mechanisms such as observation and supervised practice help youngsters learn to use tools, says Sánchez-Megías.

“Teaching events are quite rare and difficult to study because only so many learning attempts are needed until an individual learns a behaviour,” says Elliot Howard-Spink at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior in Germany. “Showing across many forms of tool use that these tool transfers are indicative of a very simple form of teaching is very cool and nice.”

During the observed interactions, the researchers noted that the teacher was forgoing food for the learning youngster’s benefit.

“This is an important observation because it fits the criteria for teaching used in animal behaviour research – that the behaviour benefits the pupil’s opportunities to learn, and is done despite having a cost to the teacher,” says Andrew Whiten at the University of St Andrews, UK.

articles.personality_title: Wild chimpanzees pass tools to teach young how to fish for food
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long wondered how chimpanzees learn to use tools like sticks to catch ants or algae. While it was known that chimps use tools, it was unclear if they teach these skills or just learn by watching.

**What happened** – Researchers at the University of Barcelona studied videos from camera traps in Senegal taken between 2017 and 2025. They recorded 33 times when adult chimpanzees handed tools directly to younger chimpanzees. In some cases, mothers gave sticks to their babies and helped them learn to gather ants or algae. They also watched older chimpanzees guide infants in cracking open baobab fruits using stones.

**Impact** – This is one of the first clear examples of wild chimpanzees actively teaching their young. Teaching means the adult chimpanzees gave up food or effort to help the younger ones learn, not just letting them watch. This shows chimpanzees have a simple but real form of passing knowledge, which helps us understand how animal cultures and intelligence develop.

**What's next step** – Researchers plan to continue observing chimpanzees to see how often teaching happens and if it changes between groups. This could reveal more about how animal learning works and how culture spreads among wild animals.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Wild chimpanzees have been seen handing tools to their young as a way of teaching important skills for finding food, showing active cultural learning in animals.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les chimpanzés sauvages transmettent des outils à leurs petits pour leur apprendre à pêcher la nourriture
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques se demandaient comment les chimpanzés apprennent à utiliser des outils comme des bâtons pour attraper des fourmis ou des algues. On savait qu’ils utilisaient des outils, mais on ignorait s’ils enseignaient ces compétences ou s’ils apprenaient simplement en observant.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université de Barcelone ont étudié des vidéos prises entre 2017 et 2025 au Sénégal. Ils ont enregistré 33 cas où des chimpanzés adultes ont remis des outils directement à des jeunes. Parfois, des mères donnaient des bâtons à leurs bébés et les aidaient à attraper des fourmis ou des algues. Ils ont aussi vu des chimpanzés plus âgés guider des petits pour casser des fruits de baobab avec des pierres.

**Impact** – C’est l’un des premiers exemples clairs de chimpanzés sauvages qui enseignent activement à leurs jeunes. Enseigner signifie que les adultes renoncent à de la nourriture ou font un effort pour aider les petits à apprendre, pas seulement les laisser regarder. Cela montre que les chimpanzés ont une forme simple mais réelle de transmission de connaissances, ce qui nous aide à mieux comprendre le développement de la culture et de l’intelligence animale.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à observer les chimpanzés pour savoir à quelle fréquence l’enseignement a lieu et s’il change selon les groupes. Cela pourrait révéler davantage sur la manière dont les animaux apprennent et comment la culture se transmet parmi eux.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les chimpanzés sauvages transmettent des outils à leurs petits pour leur apprendre à chercher de la nourriture, montrant un apprentissage culturel actif chez les animaux.
articles.personality_title_es: Chimpancés salvajes entregan herramientas a sus crías para enseñarles a pescar comida
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han querido saber cómo los chimpancés aprenden a usar herramientas como palos para atrapar hormigas o algas. Se sabía que usaban herramientas, pero no si enseñaban estas habilidades o solo aprendían observando.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Barcelona analizaron videos tomados entre 2017 y 2025 en Senegal. Registraron 33 ocasiones en que chimpancés adultos entregaron herramientas directamente a los jóvenes. En algunos casos, las madres daban palos a sus crías y las ayudaban a atrapar hormigas o algas. También vieron chimpancés mayores guiar a los bebés para abrir frutos de baobab con piedras.

**Impacto** – Este es uno de los primeros ejemplos claros de chimpancés salvajes que enseñan activamente a sus crías. Enseñar significa que los adultos renunciaron a comida o hicieron un esfuerzo para ayudar a los jóvenes a aprender, no solo dejarlos observar. Esto muestra que los chimpancés tienen una forma simple pero real de transmitir conocimientos, ayudándonos a entender mejor cómo se desarrolla la cultura y la inteligencia animal.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán observando a los chimpancés para ver con qué frecuencia ocurre la enseñanza y si varía entre grupos. Esto podría revelar más sobre cómo aprenden los animales y cómo se transmite la cultura entre ellos.

**Frase clave** – Los chimpancés salvajes entregan herramientas a sus crías para enseñarles a buscar comida, mostrando un aprendizaje cultural activo en los animales.
